name: Tasimelteon
lead: Tasimelteon is a prescription melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist developed by Vanda Pharmaceuticals and sold as Hetlioz. The US FDA approved it in January 2014 for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder in adults, and in December 2020 for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[1][2][11]

Its link to appearance is through sleep and recovery: a drug that helps the body clock line up with the day and night aims to give a regular sleep window, and people interested in looking rested, in skin and face quality, and in training recovery treat consistent sleep as a foundation. Published work on tasimelteon itself concerns sleep and circadian outcomes; no study has measured appearance outcomes.

Non-24 is a circadian rhythm disorder mainly affecting totally blind people. Phase 3 trials in totally blind people (SET and RESET) reported entrainment of the circadian rhythm in a proportion of patients on treatment,[3][12] a phase 2/3 programme examined transient insomnia after a shift in sleep time in healthy volunteers,[4] and a 2025 phase 3 trial reported on primary insomnia.[13]

paras: The US label indicates tasimelteon for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder (Non-24) in adults.[2] A later approval covers nighttime sleep disturbance in Smith-Magenis syndrome in patients aged 3 and older.[1] The label states that the mechanism by which it works in Non-24 is unclear but that MT1 and MT2 receptors are thought to be involved in controlling circadian rhythms.[2]

Wikipedia reports that the FDA clarified in October 2014 that the approved use covers both blind and sighted people with Non-24, while the EU approval in July 2015 covered only totally blind adults.[11] Public Citizen had argued that the original label omitted that the studies were in totally blind people.[11]

The most common reactions on the label (above 5 percent and at least twice as frequent as with placebo) were headache, raised alanine aminotransferase, nightmares or unusual dreams, and upper respiratory or urinary tract infection.[2] The label warns of somnolence and advises patients to limit activity after taking it to preparing for bed.[2] A randomized trial examined simulated driving performance in healthy adults after night-time administration.[18] Postmarketing pregnancy reports are insufficient to assess risk, and Wikipedia notes rodent findings at doses above the human dose.[2][11]

Tasimelteon is an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors, which are densely expressed in the brain's circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus.[2][5] It is extensively metabolised in the liver, mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, and dedicated pharmacokinetic studies examined renal and hepatic impairment, smoking, and interacting drugs.[1][6][7][8][14] An absolute bioavailability study in 14 healthy volunteers compared a capsule with an intravenous infusion.[15]

The compound was known as BMS-214,778 and was first studied for insomnia and other sleep disorders, with phase 3 trials in 2006 and 2008.[11] In 2010 the FDA granted it orphan drug status for Non-24 in totally blind adults.[11] Vanda submitted its New Drug Application in May 2013, and the FDA approved Hetlioz on 31 January 2014, the first approved treatment for Non-24.[11][15] The European Medicines Agency accepted the filing in June 2014 and the EU approval followed in July 2015.[11] In December 2020 the FDA extended the approval to sleep disturbance in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[11]

Tasimelteon is not marketed for appearance. The link people draw runs through sleep: a consistent sleep window supports recovery from training and is associated by many people with a rested look and better skin, so those who focus on sleep as a foundation for looking their best take interest in circadian-rhythm drugs. For people with Non-24 or Smith-Magenis syndrome the prescribed use is to align the sleep-wake cycle with the day-night cycle, and published work measures sleep and circadian outcomes rather than skin or facial appearance.[2][3]

Tasimelteon belongs to the melatonin receptor agonist class, which also includes ramelteon (approved 2005), melatonin as a prescription product (2007) and agomelatine (2009).[11] Reviews of melatonin receptors describe tasimelteon as a high-affinity MT1/MT2 agonist among the most advanced melatonergic drug candidates.[5] Wikipedia lists its formula as C15H19NO2, protein binding of roughly 89 to 90 percent, an elimination half-life of about 0.9 to 1.7 hours, metabolism mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, and excretion mostly in urine.[11]

Tasimelteon is prescription-only in the United States and the European Union and is sold as Hetlioz (capsules) and Hetlioz LQ (oral suspension). In the US the capsule is indicated for Smith-Magenis sleep disturbance from age 16 and the suspension from age 3 to 15, and the two forms are not interchangeable.[11] Wikipedia reports that rodent studies showed fertility impairment, certain tumours and developmental toxicity at high doses.[11]

A 2026 news report describes a phase 3 trial of tasimelteon in delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, in which the sleep timing of the body clock is shifted later than desired.[16] A small early-phase trial in REM sleep behaviour disorder was terminated.[10]

Two randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, SET and RESET, studied totally blind people with Non-24 and were published in The Lancet in 2015.[3] Earlier phase 2 and phase 3 trials examined transient insomnia after a shift in sleep time in healthy volunteers.[4] A 2025 multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 322 patients with primary insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep used polysomnography over a 5-week treatment interval to examine two tasimelteon doses against placebo.[13] A double-blind randomised trial with an open-label extension studied sleep in Smith-Magenis syndrome.[17]
Further registered trials include phase 1 pharmacokinetic studies and a paediatric study.[6][7][9] No studies were found on tasimelteon for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A prescription circadian drug approved for non-24-hour disorder in blind people; no appearance evidence.
card.note: Approved only for Non-24 and Smith-Magenis sleep disturbance.

quick.overview:
Tasimelteon is a melatonin-receptor drug approved in the US for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder, mainly seen in totally blind people, and for sleep problems in Smith-Magenis syndrome.

It is not an insomnia pill in general, and no research ties it to appearance.
quick.mechanism: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors involved in circadian timing; the label says exactly how it works in Non-24 is unclear.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, raised liver enzyme ALT, vivid dreams or nightmares and infections. The label warns of somnolence. It is prescription-only.

chain: Activates MT1/MT2 receptors involved in circadian timing
Helps align the sleep-wake cycle (in disorders of circadian rhythm)
More regular sleep, which supports recovery, skin and a rested look
angle.text: Tasimelteon is a prescription drug for circadian rhythm sleep disorders. Where it works for a person, the outcome is a more regular sleep pattern, the starting point for the recovery and rested appearance that sleep-focused looksmaxxers pursue. It is prescribed for specific diagnoses.
